BANGKOK -- An appeals court Monday upheld the conviction of an opposition lawmaker for defaming Thailand's monarchy in social media posts but reduced her prison sentence from six years to three. Rukchanok Srinork of the People’s Party was initially charged with lese majeste and violating the Computer Crime Act. In 2023, she was convicted and sentenced to six years in prison over two social media posts.
The lese majeste law, also known as Article 112 of the Criminal Code, is controversial not only because it has been used to punish things as simple as liking a post on Facebook, but also because anyone — not just royals or the authorities — can lodge a complaint that most of the time leads to detention during lengthy legal proceedings. A conviction of defaming the monarchy carries a prison term of up to 15 years, and critics say the law has often been used to quash political dissent. Student-led pro-democracy demonstrations starting in 2020 sought reforms of the lese majeste law, but the protesters became targets of the law. Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, a law advocacy group, says more than 290 people, many of them student activists, have been charged with violating Article 112 since early 2020.
The court’s decision, though expected, underlines that Thailand’s political establishment remains conservative and is sensitive about any perceived threats to the status of the country’s monarchy.

Thailand's Appeals Court has upheld a three-year prison sentence for Move Forward Party MP Rakchanok 'Ice' Srinok for royal defamation and Computer Crime Act violations related to tweets posted in 2021. The ruling confirms the lower court's decision that digital evidence proved she authored the posts criticizing the monarchy and the government's vaccine policy, rejecting her defense that the account may have been hacked. The MP was granted bail pending further appeal but must adhere to strict conditions prohibiting similar online activity.

On November 23, 2026, the Criminal Court heard the Appeals Court's ruling in royal defamation case No. A.683/2022, where the public prosecutor charged Ms. Rakchanok Srinok, a Move Forward Party list-MP, with violating Section 112 of the Criminal Code and the Computer Crime Act. The charges stemmed from two posts and retweets on her X (Twitter) account in July 2021 containing content deemed to defame the monarchy and relating to the COVID-19 vaccine administration of the former Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha's government. The defendant denied the charges and was granted bail.

On December 13, 2023, the Court of First Instance found her guilty, ruling that digital evidence and witness testimony confirmed the X account belonged to her, and her defense that the account may have been hacked lacked supporting evidence. She was sentenced to three years per count, totaling six years, without suspension. The court later granted temporary release on 500,000 baht bail with conditions prohibiting similar actions, allowing her to retain her MP status pending appeal.

Outside the court this morning, supporters including family of Party Leader Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut gathered to offer encouragement. The Appeals Court affirmed the lower court's judgment, finding the prosecution's witnesses and digital evidence credible, and rejecting the defendant's appeal arguments. jina.title: Less than majestic: the application of Thailand’s royal defamation law
jina.snippet:
In January, a 64-year-old former public servant, Anchan Preelert, was sentenced to more than 43 years’ jail– the harshest penalty ever awarded under a draconian royal defamation (lèse majesté)law. Her crime was to share[recordings](https://www.khaosodenglish.com/politics/2021/01/19/for-sharing-anti-monarchy-audio-clips-woman-gets-43-years-in-jail) criticising the late King Bhumibol and the then-Crown Prince Vajiralongkorn on social media in 2014 and 2015.

It is almost certain that Anchan will get a royal pardon in due course. And, like most of those charged, she chose to plead guilty– thereby halving her sentence from what would otherwise have been 87 years. But she could still be behind bars longer than some murderers, for whom the typical sentence ranges from[five to twenty](https://www.economist.com/asia/2017/05/18/thailands-junta-intensifies-its-hunt-for-critics-of-the-monarchy) years.

The case has drawn the world’s attention to what is known formally as[Section 112](https://library.siam-legal.com/thai-law/criminal-code-royal-family-sections-107-112) of Thailand’s Criminal Code, which states “Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir apparent or the Regent shall be punished with imprisonment of three years to fifteen years.”

Thailand is not alone in having a[lèse majesté law](https://www.osac.gov/Content/Report/e48a9599-9258-483c-9cd4-169f9c8946f5). But its penalties are by far the harshest; and many European countries don’t enforce the law. Moreover, in Thailand, the law is applied for each offence, meaning people like Anchan can face sentences of several decades– previously, the longest sentence was[35 years](https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/general/1265778/longest-prison-sentence-ever-for-lese-majeste). Further,[anyone](https://www.bangkokpost.com/opinion/opinion/292365/will-ah-kong-death-reignites-debates-on-lese-majeste-law) can file a lèse majesté complaint, which police usually feel duty bound to follow up. keenable.title: Thai court upholds royal defamation conviction for opposition lawmaker and cuts sentence to 3 years
keenable.snippet:
BANGKOK -- An appeals court Monday upheld the conviction of an opposition lawmaker for defaming Thailand's monarchy in social media posts but reduced her prison sentence from six years to three.
Rukchanok Srinork of the People’s Party was initially charged with lese majeste and violating the Computer Crime Act. In 2023, [she was convicted and sentenced](https://apnews.com/article/thailand-defaming-monarchy-rukchanok-5714eea2b3a55df891de9b4e658366ac) to six years in prison over two social media posts.
The appeals court said in a statement that it upheld the conviction in connection with one post but dropped the charges related to the other, halving her sentence. It said the three-year penalty was imposed under the lese majeste law, which carries a heavier penalty than the Computer Crime Act, a broad law regulating online activities.

People’s Party leader Natthaphong Reungpanyawut said the court dropped the charges on one post due to insufficient evidence. He said they would appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court and seek bail for Rukchanok.
If her request for a bail release is not approved and she is sent to prison, she would immediately be removed from her seat in Parliament.
The two posts were shared in 2021 on X, then known as Twitter. One reportedly criticized the monarchy over its links to a coronavirus vaccine, while the other was a repost of an anti-monarchy message. Rukchanok has denied writing the posts herself.

The lese majeste law, also known as Article 112 of the Criminal Code, is controversial not only because it has been used to punish things as simple as liking a post on Facebook, but also because anyone — not just royals or the authorities — can lodge a complaint that most of the time leads to detention during lengthy legal proceedings.
A conviction of defaming the monarchy carries a prison term of up to 15 years, and critics say the law has often been used to quash political dissent.

BANGKOK, Nov 23 - Thailand's Appeals Court on Monday halved a six-year jail sentence imposed on an opposition lawmaker over a social media post deemed to have insulted the country's powerful monarchy.
Thailand has among the strictest lese majeste laws in the world, with jail terms of up to 15 years for each case of defaming, insulting or threatening the king, queen, heir apparent or regent.
People's Party lawmaker Rukchanok Srinork, a former activist known locally as "Ice", was sentenced by a lower court in 2023 to six years in prison over an X post she made in 2021 and another that she shared, in violation of lese majeste and computer crimes laws.
The court on Monday said it acquitted her of sharing the post and halved the jail term.

keenable.title: A Thai court sentences an opposition lawmaker to 2 years in prison for defaming the monarchy
keenable.snippet:
BANGKOK (AP) — A Thai court on Monday sentenced a lawmaker from a progressive opposition party to two years in prison after finding her guilty of defaming the monarchy in a speech she made during a protest rally three years ago.
[Chonthicha Jangrew](https://apnews.com/article/thailand-election-democratic-reform-protests-050701f4f2d2367efa3f3a8d94feca88) of the Move Forward Party was greeted by several supporters when she arrived at the Thanyaburi Provincial Court in Pathum Thani province, north of Bangkok, with some party colleagues. Chonthicha, popularly known by her nickname “Lookkate,” represents a constituency in Pathum Thani.
Her charges stemmed from her speech in 2021 that demanded the release of all political prisoners during a rally in front of the same court that delivered Monday’s sentence.
She was found guilty for parts of the speech concerning how the government then led by Prime Minister Prayuth Chan-ocha had amended laws to give King Vajiralongkorn more power to control the palace wealth, which is managed by the Crown Property Bureau.
The judge said her speech could misinform the public by suggesting that King Vajiralongkorn can spend taxpayers’ money for his personal use and use his influence to interfere with politics, which could tarnish his reputation.
The judge originally sentenced her to three years in prison, but reduced it to two years because of her cooperation in the trial. The law for defaming the monarchy, an offense known as lese majeste, carries a penalty of three to 15 years imprisonment. It is widely referred to as Article 112 from its place in the Criminal Code.

BANGKOK, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Thailand's Appeals Court on Monday halved a six-year jail sentence imposed on an opposition lawmaker over a social media post deemed to have insulted the country's powerful monarchy.
Thailand has among the strictest lese majeste laws in the world, with jail terms of up to 15 years for each case of defaming, insulting or threatening the king, queen, heir apparent or regent.

BANGKOK -- An appeals court Monday upheld the conviction of an opposition lawmaker for defaming Thailand's monarchy in social media posts but reduced her prison sentence from six years to three. Rukchanok Srinork of the People’s Party was initially charged with lese majeste and violating the Computer Crime Act. In 2023, she was convicted and sentenced to six years in prison over two social media posts.
The lese majeste law, also known as Article 112 of the Criminal Code, is controversial not only because it has been used to punish things as simple as liking a post on Facebook, but also because anyone — not just royals or the authorities — can lodge a complaint that most of the time leads to detention during lengthy legal proceedings. A conviction of defaming the monarchy carries a prison term of up to 15 years, and critics say the law has often been used to quash political dissent. Student-led pro-democracy demonstrations starting in 2020 sought reforms of the lese majeste law, but the protesters became targets of the law. Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, a law advocacy group, says more than 290 people, many of them student activists, have been charged with violating Article 112 since early 2020.
The court’s decision, though expected, underlines that Thailand’s political establishment remains conservative and is sensitive about any perceived threats to the status of the country’s monarchy.
